question: Which AWS service sets up and governs a multi-account environment based on best practices, including a landing zone, guardrails (controls), and Account Factory?
option_a: AWS Control Tower
option_b: AWS Service Catalog
option_c: AWS Config
option_d: AWS Resource Access Manager
explanation: Control Tower automates a well-architected multi-account landing zone with preventive and detective controls and an Account Factory for vending new accounts.

question: A company has 120 VPCs across 30 accounts in one Region that all need to communicate with each other and with on-premises networks over AWS Direct Connect. VPC peering has become unmanageable. Which solution simplifies connectivity at scale?
option_a: AWS Transit Gateway shared through AWS RAM, with a Direct Connect gateway associated with the transit gateway
option_b: A full mesh of VPC peering connections
option_c: A Site-to-Site VPN from each VPC to on premises
option_d: AWS PrivateLink endpoint services for every VPC
explanation: Transit Gateway is a hub that connects thousands of VPCs and on-premises networks with transitive routing; sharing it with AWS RAM lets other accounts attach, and a Direct Connect gateway connects it to on premises through a transit VIF.
services: AWS Transit Gateway;AWS Resource Access Manager;AWS Direct Connect

question: A company wants application teams in separate accounts to deploy into subnets of a centrally managed VPC owned by the networking account, without managing their own VPCs. Which approach should it use?
option_a: Share the subnets with the application accounts using AWS RAM (VPC sharing)
option_b: Create VPC peering from each account
option_c: Give the application teams IAM users in the networking account
option_d: Use AWS Transit Gateway Connect attachments
explanation: VPC sharing through AWS Resource Access Manager lets participant accounts launch resources into shared subnets while the owner account manages the VPC, route tables, and gateways.

question: A company wants every new account created through its landing zone to automatically get a standard set of IAM roles, AWS Config rules, and a baseline VPC across all governed Regions. Which mechanism deploys these resources consistently to new accounts?
option_a: CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment to the target OUs
option_b: Manually running a CloudFormation stack in each new account
option_c: AWS Systems Manager Run Command
option_d: IAM Access Analyzer
explanation: Service-managed StackSets integrated with AWS Organizations can automatically deploy stacks to accounts as they are added to target OUs, across multiple Regions.

question: A company's finance team needs to allocate shared Savings Plans discounts and present showback reports per business unit, while the management account remains the payer. Which approach provides this with the least custom tooling?
option_a: Enforce cost allocation tags with tag policies and use AWS Cost Categories with the Cost and Usage Report or Cost Explorer for showback
option_b: Create a separate AWS Organization for each business unit
option_c: Disable Savings Plans sharing
option_d: Build a custom billing system from CloudTrail logs
explanation: Tag policies standardize tags, Cost Categories group costs by business rules, and CUR/Cost Explorer report spend (including amortized Savings Plans) per category without custom pipelines.
services: AWS Organizations;AWS Cost Explorer;AWS Cost and Usage Report

question: A company needs on-premises servers to resolve private DNS names of resources in multiple VPCs, and VPC resources must resolve names in the on-premises domain corp.example.com. What should a solutions architect configure?
option_a: Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints for on-premises queries and outbound endpoints with forwarding rules for corp.example.com, shared with other accounts through AWS RAM
option_b: Public hosted zones for all private resources
option_c: An EC2-based DNS server in each VPC with no forwarding
option_d: VPC peering with DNS resolution disabled
explanation: Inbound Resolver endpoints receive queries from on premises; outbound endpoints with forwarding rules send queries for on-premises domains to on-premises DNS. Resolver rules can be shared across accounts with RAM.

question: A company must apply consistent AWS WAF rules and security group policies across hundreds of accounts, and automatically apply them to newly created resources. Which service should it use?
option_a: AWS Firewall Manager with AWS Organizations
option_b: AWS Config conformance packs only
option_c: AWS Shield Standard
option_d: IAM Access Analyzer
explanation: Firewall Manager centrally configures and enforces WAF, Shield Advanced, security group, Network Firewall, and DNS Firewall policies across an organization, including for new resources.

question: A company wants a central security team to manage GuardDuty, Security Hub, and IAM Access Analyzer for all accounts without using the management account for day-to-day operations. What should it configure?
option_a: Register a dedicated security tooling account as the delegated administrator for each service
option_b: Enable each service separately in every account and log in to each
option_c: Use the management account as the administrator for all services
option_d: Create IAM users for security engineers in every account
explanation: Delegated administration lets a member account (commonly a security tooling account) manage organization-wide security services, following the best practice of minimizing use of the management account.

question: A company has a hub-and-spoke network with Transit Gateway. Security requires that all traffic between spoke VPCs and to the internet be inspected by a stateful firewall in a central inspection VPC, with symmetric routing across Availability Zones. Which design meets these requirements?
option_a: Deploy AWS Network Firewall in an inspection VPC attached to the transit gateway, use separate TGW route tables for spokes and inspection, and enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment
option_b: Put security groups on each spoke VPC's instances
option_c: Use VPC peering between spokes with network ACLs
option_d: Deploy a NAT gateway in each spoke VPC
explanation: Routing spoke traffic through an inspection VPC with Network Firewall centralizes stateful inspection; appliance mode keeps both directions of a flow in the same AZ to avoid asymmetric routing that breaks stateful inspection.

question: A company operates two Direct Connect locations and requires that on-premises connectivity to AWS survives the failure of a single device or a single Direct Connect location, at the lowest cost that still meets AWS high-resiliency recommendations. Which design should it use?
option_a: Two dedicated connections, each terminating on separate devices in two different Direct Connect locations
option_b: One connection with a backup Site-to-Site VPN in the same location
option_c: Two connections on the same device in one location
option_d: One hosted connection and no backup
explanation: AWS's high resiliency model uses one connection at each of two locations on separate devices, surviving device and location failures. Maximum resiliency doubles this (two per location) for critical workloads.

question: A SaaS provider must expose an internal service running behind a Network Load Balancer to hundreds of customer VPCs. Customer CIDR ranges overlap with each other and with the provider's network, and traffic must stay private. Which solution meets these requirements?
option_a: Create a VPC endpoint service (AWS PrivateLink) for the NLB and have customers create interface endpoints in their VPCs
option_b: Peer the provider VPC with each customer VPC
option_c: Attach all customer VPCs to the provider's transit gateway
option_d: Expose the service publicly and restrict with security groups
explanation: PrivateLink provides private, unidirectional access through interface endpoints with IPs in the consumer's VPC, so overlapping CIDRs are not a problem. Peering and Transit Gateway require non-overlapping CIDRs.

question: A company wants to prevent developers in sandbox accounts from launching expensive GPU instance types and from creating resources without a 'CostCenter' tag. Controls must be preventive and centrally managed. What should a solutions architect implement?
option_a: SCPs on the sandbox OU that deny ec2:RunInstances for disallowed instance types (ec2:InstanceType condition) and deny creation requests that lack the CostCenter tag (aws:RequestTag condition)
option_b: AWS Budgets alerts for each sandbox account
option_c: AWS Config rules that delete untagged resources after creation
option_d: An IAM policy for each developer user in every account
explanation: SCPs with condition keys centrally prevent disallowed actions across all principals in the OU. Budgets and Config rules are detective or reactive rather than preventive.

question: A company acquired another business with its own AWS Organization of 40 accounts. The company wants to bring the accounts into its organization with minimal disruption and keep workloads running. What is the correct approach?
option_a: Remove each account from the acquired organization (ensuring standalone billing details are in place), then accept invitations from the acquiring organization, and apply SCPs after testing in a staging OU
option_b: Merge the two management accounts
option_c: Move the acquired organization's management account into the acquiring organization as a member while it still has members
option_d: Recreate all workloads in new accounts
explanation: Accounts can belong to only one organization. Each must leave its current organization (which requires standalone account information such as a payment method) and then accept an invitation. Applying SCPs carefully avoids breaking workloads.

question: Workloads in 50 accounts need centrally managed IP address allocation that prevents overlapping CIDRs as new VPCs are created, with compliance monitoring of IP usage. Which service should a solutions architect use?
option_a: Amazon VPC IP Address Manager (IPAM) integrated with AWS Organizations, with pools allocated by Region and environment
option_b: A shared spreadsheet maintained by the network team
option_c: AWS Config rules only
option_d: Route 53 Resolver
explanation: VPC IPAM plans, allocates, tracks, and monitors IP addresses across accounts and Regions, and can enforce allocation from pools so CIDRs do not overlap.

question: A company with 200 accounts wants workforce users to sign in with its Okta identity provider and receive permissions in each account based on group membership, with no IAM users. Which TWO steps are required? (Choose TWO.)
option_a: Connect Okta as the external identity provider for AWS IAM Identity Center, with automatic provisioning (SCIM) of users and groups
option_b: Create permission sets and assign groups to accounts in IAM Identity Center
option_c: Create an IAM user for each employee in each account
option_d: Configure Amazon Cognito user pools for employees
option_e: Create IAM access keys for each Okta group
explanation: Identity Center federates with Okta and can sync users and groups via SCIM; permission sets assigned to groups per account create the roles that users receive when they sign in.

question: A company needs to centralize logs from all accounts: CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and AWS Config history must be stored in one place that account administrators cannot alter. Which design best meets this requirement?
option_a: A dedicated log archive account with S3 buckets that receive logs from all accounts, protected by bucket policies, SCPs that prevent changes to logging configuration, and S3 Object Lock
option_b: Store logs in each account's own S3 bucket
option_c: Send all logs to a single CloudWatch Logs group in the management account without restrictions
option_d: Email daily log exports to the security team
explanation: A separate log archive account isolates logs from workload administrators; SCPs prevent disabling logging, and Object Lock prevents deletion. This is the pattern used by AWS Control Tower landing zones.

question: A company's accounts must use only approved AMIs, instance types, and configurations, and developers should be able to launch standard products themselves without broad IAM permissions. Which solution fits best?
option_a: Publish approved products as AWS Service Catalog portfolios shared to the organization's OUs, with launch constraints that use a role with the needed permissions
option_b: Give developers AdministratorAccess and audit monthly
option_c: Create a wiki page with approved AMI IDs
option_d: Use AWS Marketplace private offers
explanation: Service Catalog lets administrators publish approved, governed products; launch constraints let users launch products with a provisioning role rather than needing those permissions themselves.

question: A global enterprise is designing its multi-account network. Requirements: VPCs in four Regions must communicate with each other and with 12 branch offices; segmentation must keep production, development, and shared-services traffic separate; routing policies must be managed centrally from a single policy document; and the networking team is small. Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational effort?
option_a: AWS Cloud WAN with a core network policy that defines segments for production, development, and shared services, connecting VPCs and branch offices (through Site-to-Site VPN or SD-WAN Connect attachments) in all four Regions
option_b: A transit gateway in each Region with manually managed inter-Region peering and separate route tables in each
option_c: A full mesh of VPC peering connections across Regions and a VPN from every VPC to every branch
option_d: AWS PrivateLink endpoints between every pair of VPCs
explanation: Cloud WAN provides a centrally managed global network with segments defined in one policy document, and automates attachments and routing across Regions. Multiple transit gateways work but require more manual peering and route management, and peering meshes do not scale.

question: A company is building a landing zone for 300 accounts. Requirements: preventive controls stop anyone from disabling security services; detective controls flag non-compliant resources; new accounts get baselines automatically; and production and non-production accounts get different policies. Which THREE actions meet these requirements? (Choose THREE.)
option_a: Organize accounts into OUs by environment (for example, Production, Non-Production, Security) and attach different SCPs to each OU
option_b: Use AWS Control Tower with its preventive and detective controls and Account Factory for new accounts
option_c: Deploy AWS Config conformance packs or Control Tower detective controls organization-wide
option_d: Place all accounts in the root OU and use one IAM policy in each account
option_e: Rely only on monthly manual reviews
option_f: Use the management account to host production workloads
explanation: OUs let policies differ by environment, Control Tower provides account vending with baseline controls, and Config-based detective controls flag non-compliance. A flat structure, manual reviews, and workloads in the management account go against multi-account best practices.

question: A financial company has a security account with GuardDuty and Security Hub as delegated administrator. It wants high-severity findings in any account to automatically open a ticket, notify the on-call channel, and, for findings of compromised EC2 instances, isolate the instance by replacing its security groups—all without custom polling. Which design meets these requirements?
option_a: In the security account, create EventBridge rules on Security Hub findings filtered by severity that target an SNS topic and the ticketing integration, and a Step Functions workflow (or Lambda) that assumes a cross-account role to apply an isolation security group to the affected instance
option_b: Have each account's administrator check the GuardDuty console daily
option_c: Export findings weekly to S3 and process them with Athena
option_d: Disable GuardDuty in member accounts to reduce noise
explanation: Security Hub sends findings to EventBridge in the administrator account, so rules can trigger notifications, tickets, and automated remediation workflows that use cross-account roles. Manual checks and weekly exports are too slow for incident response.
services: AWS Security Hub;Amazon EventBridge;AWS Step Functions

question: A company runs hundreds of microservices across 60 accounts. Teams need to share specific services with each other privately, services must be discoverable by name, connectivity must not require network-level routing between all VPCs, and IP ranges overlap in some accounts. Which approach best meets these requirements?
option_a: Use Amazon VPC Lattice service networks shared with AWS RAM, associating VPCs and services, with auth policies controlling which services can call each other
option_b: Peer all VPCs and use Route 53 private hosted zones
option_c: Attach all VPCs to one transit gateway with a single route table
option_d: Expose all services publicly behind ALBs
explanation: VPC Lattice connects services across VPCs and accounts at the application layer without routing between VPCs, works with overlapping CIDRs, provides service discovery, and uses IAM-based auth policies. Peering and Transit Gateway require unique CIDRs and full network routing.
services: Amazon VPC Lattice;AWS Resource Access Manager

question: A company's management account currently runs production workloads, and dozens of IAM users have access to it. Auditors flagged this as a high risk because SCPs don't apply to the management account. The company wants to fix this with minimal workload disruption. What should a solutions architect recommend?
option_a: Migrate the workloads to new member accounts in a production OU, restrict management-account access to a small break-glass group through IAM Identity Center, and use delegated administrators for organization services
option_b: Attach an SCP to the management account that denies all actions
option_c: Delete the organization and recreate it from a member account
option_d: Move the management account into an OU
explanation: SCPs never restrict the management account, so best practice is to keep it free of workloads and tightly controlled, delegating service administration to member accounts. The management account cannot be moved into an OU or restricted by SCPs.

question: A company has a central Transit Gateway in us-east-1 and plans to expand into eu-west-1. Requirements: VPCs in both Regions must communicate; the on-premises data center (connected through Direct Connect to us-east-1) must reach VPCs in both Regions; and inter-Region traffic must stay on the AWS backbone. Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Choose TWO.)
option_a: Create a transit gateway in eu-west-1 and establish inter-Region transit gateway peering with the us-east-1 transit gateway, updating static routes
option_b: Associate the Direct Connect gateway with both transit gateways using transit VIFs, or route on-premises traffic through the peering
option_c: Create public VIFs to reach eu-west-1 VPC private IP addresses
option_d: Use VPC peering between every us-east-1 and eu-west-1 VPC
option_e: Route inter-Region traffic over the internet through NAT gateways
explanation: Inter-Region TGW peering carries traffic over the AWS global network (peering attachments use static routes), and a Direct Connect gateway can associate with transit gateways in multiple Regions so on premises reaches both. Public VIFs don't reach private IPs, and full peering meshes don't scale.

question: A company wants to give its 25 product teams autonomy to create AWS accounts on demand, but every account must be enrolled in governance, have network connectivity provisioned automatically from a central IPAM pool, and be tagged with an owner. Which solution best balances autonomy and governance?
option_a: Use AWS Control Tower Account Factory (or Account Factory for Terraform) with account customizations that allocate a CIDR from IPAM, create the VPC and Transit Gateway attachment, and apply required tags, triggered from a self-service request
option_b: Let teams create standalone accounts with personal credit cards and invite them later
option_c: Have the central team create every account manually through the console
option_d: Give each team access to the management account to create accounts
explanation: Account Factory with customizations automates compliant account vending, including networking from IPAM and tagging, while teams request accounts self-service. Standalone accounts bypass governance, manual creation is slow, and management-account access is a risk.

question: A company's AWS spend grew 40% in a quarter, and leadership wants each business unit accountable for its own costs. There are 150 accounts mapped loosely to business units, inconsistent tags, and shared resources (networking and logging) that serve all units. What should a solutions architect recommend?
option_a: Restructure OUs by business unit, enforce required tags with tag policies and SCPs, define AWS Cost Categories that split shared costs by rules, and give each unit Cost Explorer views, budgets, and anomaly detection for its category
option_b: Ask each business unit to estimate its costs manually
option_c: Move all workloads into one account to simplify billing
option_d: Turn off consolidated billing so each account pays separately
explanation: Account structure, enforced tagging, and Cost Categories (including split charge rules for shared costs) provide accurate allocation, and budgets plus anomaly detection give each unit ownership. Turning off consolidated billing loses volume discounts and shared Savings Plans.
